Besicovitch.TauPackage.index.fullDefinition: noncomputable def index : Ordinal.{u} → β   | i =>       -- `Z` is the set of points that are covered by already constructed balls       let Z := ⋃ j : { j // j < i }, ball (p.c (index j)) (p.r (index j))       -- `R` is the supremum of the radii of balls with centers not in `Z`       let R := iSup fun b : { b : β // p.c b ∉ Z } => p.r b       -- return an index `b` for which the center `c b` is not in `Z`, and the radius is at       -- least `R / τ`, if such an index exists (and garbage otherwise).       Classical.epsilon fun b : β => p.c b ∉ Z ∧ R ≤ p.τ * p.r b   termination_by i => i   decreasing_by exact j.2
Besicovitch.TauPackage.index.description: This defines a function that assigns a point in a non-empty type, based on an inductively large ordinal, within a metric space structure related to Besicovitch's framework.

Besicovitch.exist_disjoint_covering_fami.code:
Besicovitch.exist_disjoint_covering_families.{u, u_1} {α : Type u_1} [MetricSpace α] {β : Type u} {N : ℕ} {τ : ℝ}
  (hτ : 1 < τ) (hN : IsEmpty (SatelliteConfig α N τ)) (q : BallPackage β α) :
  ∃ s,
    (∀ (i : Fin N), (s i).PairwiseDisjoint fun j => closedBall (q.c j) (q.r j)) ∧
      range q.c ⊆ ⋃ i, ⋃ j ∈ s i, ball (q.c j) (q.r j)
Besicovitch.exist_disjoint_covering_fami.comment:
The topological Besicovitch covering theorem: there exist finitely many families of disjoint
balls covering all the centers in a package. More specifically, one can use `N` families if there
are no satellite configurations with `N+1` points.

Besicovitch.exist_finset_disjoint_balls_.code:
Besicovitch.exist_finset_disjoint_balls_large_measure.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [MetricSpace α] [SecondCountableTopology α]
  [MeasurableSpace α] [OpensMeasurableSpace α] (μ : Measure α) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] {N : ℕ} {τ : ℝ} (hτ : 1 < τ)
  (hN : IsEmpty (SatelliteConfig α N τ)) (s : Set α) (r : α → ℝ) (rpos : ∀ x ∈ s, 0 < r x) (rle : ∀ x ∈ s, r x ≤ 1) :
  ∃ t,
    ↑t ⊆ s ∧
      μ (s \ ⋃ x ∈ t, closedBall x (r x)) ≤ ↑N / (↑N + 1) * μ s ∧ (↑t).PairwiseDisjoint fun x => closedBall x (r x)
Besicovitch.exist_finset_disjoint_balls_.comment:
Consider, for each `x` in a set `s`, a radius `r x ∈ (0, 1]`. Then one can find finitely
many disjoint balls of the form `closedBall x (r x)` covering a proportion `1/(N+1)` of `s`, if
there are no satellite configurations with `N+1` points.

there are no satellite configurations with `N+1` points.

Besicovitch.vitaliFamily.fullDefinition: protected def vitaliFamily (μ : Measure α) [SFinite μ] : VitaliFamily μ where   setsAt x := (fun r : ℝ => closedBall x r) '' Ioi (0 : ℝ)   measurableSet _ := forall_mem_image.2 fun _ _ ↦ isClosed_ball.measurableSet   nonempty_interior _ := forall_mem_image.2 fun r rpos ↦     (nonempty_ball.2 rpos).mono ball_subset_interior_closedBall   nontrivial x ε εpos := ⟨closedBall x ε, mem_image_of_mem _ εpos, Subset.rfl⟩   covering := by     intro s f fsubset ffine     let g : α → Set ℝ := fun x => {r | 0 < r ∧ closedBall x r ∈ f x}     have A : ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ δ > 0, (g x ∩ Ioo 0 δ).Nonempty := by       intro x xs δ δpos       obtain ⟨t, tf, ht⟩ : ∃ (t : Set α), t ∈ f x ∧ t ⊆ closedBall x (δ / 2) :=         ffine x xs (δ / 2) (half_pos δpos)       obtain ⟨r, rpos, rfl⟩ : ∃ r : ℝ, 0 < r ∧ closedBall x r = t := by simpa using fsubset x xs tf       rcases le_total r (δ / 2) with (H | H)       · exact ⟨r, ⟨rpos, tf⟩, ⟨rpos, H.trans_lt (half_lt_self δpos)⟩⟩       · have : closedBall x r = closedBall x (δ / 2) :=           Subset.antisymm ht (closedBall_subset_closedBall H)         rw [this] at tf         exact ⟨δ / 2, ⟨half_pos δpos, tf⟩, ⟨half_pos δpos, half_lt_self δpos⟩⟩     obtain ⟨t, r, _, ts, tg, μt, tdisj⟩ :       ∃ (t : Set α) (r : α → ℝ),         t.Countable ∧           t ⊆ s ∧             (∀ x ∈ t, r x ∈ g x ∩ Ioo 0 1) ∧               μ (s \ ⋃ x ∈ t, closedBall x (r x)) = 0 ∧                 t.PairwiseDisjoint fun x => closedBall x (r x) :=       exists_disjoint_closedBall_covering_ae μ g s A (fun _ => 1) fun _ _ => zero_lt_one     let F : α → α × Set α := fun x => (x, closedBall x (r x))     refine ⟨F '' t, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩     · rintro - ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩; exact ts hx     · rintro p ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩ q ⟨y, hy, rfl⟩ hxy       exact tdisj hx hy (ne_of_apply_ne F hxy)     · rintro - ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩; exact (tg x hx).1.2     · rwa [biUnion_image]
Besicovitch.vitaliFamily.description: In a metric space that satisfies the Besicovitch covering property and has the requisite topological and measure-theoretic structures, the collection of closed balls with positive radii forms a Vitali family according to the measurable Besicovitch theorem.

Besicovitch.tendsto_filterAt.code:
Besicovitch.tendsto_filterAt.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [MetricSpace α] [SecondCountableTopology α] [MeasurableSpace α]
  [OpensMeasurableSpace α] [HasBesicovitchCovering α] (μ : Measure α) [SFinite μ] (x : α) :
  Tendsto (fun r => closedBall x r) (𝓝[>] 0) ((Besicovitch.vitaliFamily μ).filterAt x)
Besicovitch.tendsto_filterAt.comment:
The main feature of the Besicovitch Vitali family is that its filter at a point `x` corresponds
to convergence along closed balls. We record one of the two implications here, which will enable us
to deduce specific statements on differentiation of measures in this context from the general
versions.

Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div.code:
Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div_of_measurableSet.{u} {β : Type u} [MetricSpace β] [MeasurableSpace β]
  [BorelSpace β] [SecondCountableTopology β] [HasBesicovitchCovering β] (μ : Measure β) [IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ]
  {s : Set β} (hs : MeasurableSet s) :
  ∀ᵐ (x : β) ∂μ, Tendsto (fun r => μ (s ∩ closedBall x r) / μ (closedBall x r)) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 (s.indicator 1 x))
Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div.comment:
Given a measurable set `s`, then `μ (s ∩ closedBall x r) / μ (closedBall x r)` converges when
`r` tends to `0`, for almost every `x`. The limit is `1` for `x ∈ s` and `0` for `x ∉ s`.
This shows that almost every point of `s` is a Lebesgue density point for `s`.
A version for non-measurable sets holds, but it only gives the first conclusion,
see `ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div`.

Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div.code:
Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div.{u} {β : Type u} [MetricSpace β] [MeasurableSpace β] [BorelSpace β]
  [SecondCountableTopology β] [HasBesicovitchCovering β] (μ : Measure β) [IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ] (s : Set β) :
  ∀ᵐ (x : β) ∂μ.restrict s, Tendsto (fun r => μ (s ∩ closedBall x r) / μ (closedBall x r)) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 1)
Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div.comment:
Given an arbitrary set `s`, then `μ (s ∩ closedBall x r) / μ (closedBall x r)` converges
to `1` when `r` tends to `0`, for almost every `x` in `s`.
This shows that almost every point of `s` is a Lebesgue density point for `s`.
A stronger version holds for measurable sets, see `ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div_of_measurableSet`.

See also `IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div`.

blimsup_cthickening_mul_ae_eq.code:
blimsup_cthickening_mul_ae_eq.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [MetricSpace α] [SecondCountableTopology α] [MeasurableSpace α]
  [BorelSpace α] (μ : Measure α) [IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ] [IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure μ] (p : ℕ → Prop) (s : ℕ → Set α)
  {M : ℝ} (hM : 0 < M) (r : ℕ → ℝ) (hr : Tendsto r atTop (𝓝 0)) :
  blimsup (fun i => cthickening (M * r i) (s i)) atTop p =ᶠ[ae μ] blimsup (fun i => cthickening (r i) (s i)) atTop p
blimsup_cthickening_mul_ae_eq.comment:
Given a sequence of subsets `sᵢ` of a metric space, together with a sequence of radii `rᵢ`
such that `rᵢ → 0`, the set of points which belong to infinitely many of the closed
`rᵢ`-thickenings of `sᵢ` is unchanged almost everywhere for a uniformly locally doubling measure if
the `rᵢ` are all scaled by a positive constant.

This lemma is a generalisation of Lemma 9 appearing on page 217 of
[J.W.S. Cassels, *Some metrical theorems in Diophantine approximation. I*](cassels1950).

See also `blimsup_thickening_mul_ae_eq`.

explanatories.Besicovitch.SatelliteConfig.r: This defines a function that assigns a positive real number to each point in a finite index set related to a specific configuration in Besicovitch's satellite theory.
explanatories.dist_smul₀: This theorem states that for elements in a normed division ring and a seminormed additive group, the distance between their scalar multiples by a fixed element is proportional to the scalar's norm times the distance between the original elements.
explanatories.dist_sub_right: The distance between two elements in a pseudo-metric space remains constant when both elements are divided by the same fixed element.
explanatories.mul_left_comm: The theorem establishes that in a commutative semigroup, the multiplication operation can be rearranged among three elements without changing the result.
explanatories.Real.norm_of_nonneg: The norm of a non-negative real number is equal to the number itself.
explanatories.Besicovitch.SatelliteConfig.h: For any two distinct indices in the configuration, the positive radii associated with those indices must satisfy specific distance constraints that relate to their corresponding points in the metric space.
explanatories.Besicovitch.SatelliteConfig.hlast: For any index less than the last in the configuration, the positive radius associated with that index must satisfy certain distance constraints in relation to the point corresponding to the last index and its own radius.
explanatories.mul_add: This theorem states that in a structure where multiplication is left distributive over addition, the product of an element and the sum of two other elements equals the sum of the products of the first element with each of the other two elements.
explanatories.Besicovitch.SatelliteConfig.inter: For an index in a finite set less than the last index, the distance between the points associated with that index and the last index is bounded by the sum of their respective positive values in the configuration defined by Besicovitch's satellite theory.
explanatories.Besicovitch.SatelliteConfig.rpos: For any given index in the finite set, the positive value associated with that index in Besicovitch's satellite configuration is guaranteed to be greater than zero.
explanatories.And.left: From a conjunction of two propositions, it is possible to extract and prove the first proposition.
explanatories.And.right: This theorem allows for the extraction of the second component from a conjunction when given a proof of that conjunction.

Besicovitch.SatelliteConfig.centerAndRes.fullDefinition: def centerAndRescale : SatelliteConfig E N τ where   c i := (a.r (last N))⁻¹ • (a.c i - a.c (last N))   r i := (a.r (last N))⁻¹ * a.r i   rpos i := by positivity   h i j hij := by     simp (disch := positivity) only [dist_smul₀, dist_sub_right, mul_left_comm τ,       Real.norm_of_nonneg]     rcases a.h hij with (⟨H₁, H₂⟩ | ⟨H₁, H₂⟩) <;> [left; right] <;> constructor <;> gcongr   hlast i hi := by     simp (disch := positivity) only [dist_smul₀, dist_sub_right, mul_left_comm τ,       Real.norm_of_nonneg]     have ⟨H₁, H₂⟩ := a.hlast i hi     constructor <;> gcongr   inter i hi := by     simp (disch := positivity) only [dist_smul₀, ← mul_add, dist_sub_right, Real.norm_of_nonneg]     gcongr     exact a.inter i hi
Besicovitch.SatelliteConfig.centerAndRes.description: This defines a method for rescaling a satellite configuration in a vector space such that its base point is moved to the origin and its base radius is adjusted to one.

rieszContentAux_mono.code:

  (h : K₁ ≤ K₂) : rieszContentAux Λ K₁ ≤ rieszContentAux Λ K₂
rieszContentAux_mono.comment:
Riesz content λ (associated with a positive linear functional Λ) is
monotone: if `K₁ ⊆ K₂` are compact subsets in X, then `λ(K₁) ≤ λ(K₂)`.
rieszContentAux_mono.description: The Riesz content associated with a positive linear functional is monotonic, meaning that if one compact subset is contained within another, the content of the smaller subset will not exceed that of the larger subset.

  (K : Compacts X) {ε : ℝ≥0} (εpos : 0 < ε) : ∃ f, (∀ x ∈ K, 1 ≤ f x) ∧ Λ f < rieszContentAux Λ K + ε
exists_lt_rieszContentAux_add_pos.comment:
The Riesz content can be approximated arbitrarily well by evaluating the positive linear
functional on test functions: for any `ε > 0`, there exists a bounded continuous nonnegative

`∫⁻ a in s, f a ∂μ` is defined as the supremum of integrals of simple functions

functions `φ : α →ₛ ℝ≥0`.

MeasureTheory.setLIntegral_mono_ae.comment:
Lebesgue integral over a set is monotone in function.

This version assumes that the upper estimate is an a.e. measurable function
and the estimate holds a.e. on the set.
See also `setLIntegral_mono_ae'` for a version that assumes measurability of the set
but assumes no regularity of either function.

MeasurableEmbedding.lintegral_map.comment:
If `g : α → β` is a measurable embedding and `f : β → ℝ≥0∞` is any function (not necessarily
measurable), then `∫⁻ a, f a ∂(map g μ) = ∫⁻ a, f (g a) ∂μ`. Compare with `lintegral_map` which
applies to any measurable `g : α → β` but requires that `f` is measurable as well.

MeasureTheory.lmarginal.code:
MeasureTheory.lmarginal.{u_1, u_3} {δ : Type u_1} {π : δ → Type u_3} [(x : δ) → MeasurableSpace (π x)] [DecidableEq δ]
  (μ : (i : δ) → Measure (π i)) (s : Finset δ) (f : ((i : δ) → π i) → ℝ≥0∞) (x : (i : δ) → π i) : ℝ≥0∞
MeasureTheory.lmarginal.comment:
Integrate `f(x₁,…,xₙ)` over all variables `xᵢ` where `i ∈ s`. Return a function in the
remaining variables (it will be constant in the `xᵢ` for `i ∈ s`).
This is the marginal distribution of all variables not in `s` when the considered measure
is the product measure.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.pi: This definition establishes a measure for the product of finite measurable spaces by combining the measures associated with each space into a single measure for the Cartesian product of the spaces.

MeasureTheory.lmarginal.fullDefinition: def lmarginal (μ : ∀ i, Measure (π i)) (s : Finset δ) (f : (∀ i, π i) → ℝ≥0∞)     (x : ∀ i, π i) : ℝ≥0∞ :=   ∫⁻ y : ∀ i : s, π i, f (updateFinset x s y) ∂Measure.pi fun i : s => μ i
MeasureTheory.lmarginal.description: This defines a function that computes the marginal distribution of a set of variables not included in a specified finite subset by integrating a given function over the excluded variables under a product measure.

StronglyMeasurableAtFilter.comment:
A function `f` is strongly measurable at a filter `l` w.r.t. a measure `μ` if it is
ae strongly measurable w.r.t. `μ.restrict s` for some `s ∈ l`.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable: A function is considered almost everywhere strongly measurable with respect to a measure if it is equal to the limit of a sequence of simple functions except on a set of measure zero.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.Memℒp.restrict: This theorem states that if a measurable function belongs to a certain integrability class with respect to a measure, it also belongs to the same class when considering the measure restricted to a subset.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable.restr: If a function is almost everywhere strongly measurable with respect to a measure, then it remains almost everywhere strongly measurable when the measure is restricted to a subset.

  (T : Set α → E →L[ℝ] F) {C : ℝ} (hT : DominatedFinMeasAdditive μ T C) (f : α → E) : F
MeasureTheory.setToFun.comment:
Extend `T : Set α → E →L[ℝ] F` to `(α → E) → F` (for integrable functions `α → E`). We set it to
0 if the function is not integrable.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.DominatedFinMeasAdditive: A function is defined as dominated finite measure additive if its norm on any measurable set is bounded by the measure of that set multiplied by a constant.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Integrable: The definition describes a property indicating that a function is measurable and has a finite integral with respect to a specified measure.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.L1.setToL1: This definition establishes a linear mapping that extends a dominated finite measure additive function from measurable sets to equivalence classes of integrable functions.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Integrable.toL1: An integrable function can be represented as a member of the equivalence class in the L1 space associated with the specified measure and normed additive group.

MeasureTheory.setToFun.fullDefinition: def setToFun (hT : DominatedFinMeasAdditive μ T C) (f : α → E) : F :=   if hf : Integrable f μ then L1.setToL1 hT (hf.toL1 f) else 0
MeasureTheory.setToFun.description: This definition describes a way to extend a set function for measurable sets to also act on integrable functions by returning a value based on the set function, and outputting zero for functions that are not integrable.

MeasureTheory.tendsto_setToFun_of_domina.code:
MeasureTheory.tendsto_setToFun_of_dominated_convergence.{u_1, u_2, u_3} {α : Type u_1} {E : Type u_2} {F : Type u_3}
  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] {m : MeasurableSpace α}
  {μ : Measure α} [CompleteSpace F] {T : Set α → E →L[ℝ] F} {C : ℝ} (hT : DominatedFinMeasAdditive μ T C)
  {fs : ℕ → α → E} {f : α → E} (bound : α → ℝ) (fs_measurable : ∀ (n : ℕ), AEStronglyMeasurable (fs n) μ)
  (bound_integrable : Integrable bound μ) (h_bound : ∀ (n : ℕ), ∀ᵐ (a : α) ∂μ, ‖fs n a‖ ≤ bound a)
  (h_lim : ∀ᵐ (a : α) ∂μ, Tendsto (fun n => fs n a) atTop (𝓝 (f a))) :
  Tendsto (fun n => setToFun μ T hT (fs n)) atTop (𝓝 (setToFun μ T hT f))
MeasureTheory.tendsto_setToFun_of_domina.comment:
Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem provides sufficient conditions under which almost
everywhere convergence of a sequence of functions implies the convergence of their image by
`setToFun`.
We could weaken the condition `bound_integrable` to require `HasFiniteIntegral bound μ` instead
(i.e. not requiring that `bound` is measurable), but in all applications proving integrability
is easier.

explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.setToFun: This definition describes a way to extend a set function for measurable sets to also act on integrable functions by returning a value based on the set function, and outputting zero for functions that are not integrable.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable: A function is considered almost everywhere strongly measurable with respect to a measure if it is equal to the limit of a sequence of simple functions except on a set of measure zero.

MeasureTheory.tendsto_setToFun_of_domina.description: The theorem states that if a sequence of functions converges almost everywhere and is dominated by an integrable bound, then their corresponding images under a dominated finite measure additive mapping converge to the image of the limit function.

  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedAddCommGroup F] {f : α → E} {g : α → F} {μ : Measure α} {l : Filter α}
  [l.IsMeasurablyGenerated] (hf : f =O[l] g) (hfm : StronglyMeasurableAtFilter f l μ) (hg : IntegrableAtFilter g l μ) :
  IntegrableAtFilter f l μ
Asymptotics.IsBigO.integrableAtFilter.comment:
If `f = O[l] g` on measurably generated `l`, `f` is strongly measurable at `l`,
and `g` is integrable at `l`, then `f` is integrable at `l`.

explanatories.StronglyMeasurableAtFilter: This definition specifies the condition under which a function is considered strongly measurable at a given filter in relation to a certain measure, requiring it to be almost everywhere strongly measurable under restrictions defined by the filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.IntegrableAtFilter: A function is defined to be integrable at a given filter if it is integrable on at least one of the sets contained within that filter.

Asymptotics.IsBigO.integrableAtFilter.description: This theorem asserts that if one function is asymptotically bounded by another, is strongly measurable with respect to a filter, and the second function is integrable with respect to that filter, then the first function is also integrable with respect to the same filter.

MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrableOn.integr.comment:
If `f` is locally integrable on `[a, ∞)`, and `f =O[atTop] g`, for some
`g` integrable at `atTop`, then `f` is integrable on `[a, ∞)`.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.IntegrableAtFilter: A function is defined to be integrable at a given filter if it is integrable on at least one of the sets contained within that filter.
explanatories.Filter.atTop: This definition introduces a filter that captures the behavior of elements approaching infinity in an ordered set, generated by all sets containing elements greater than or equal to any given element.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.IntegrableOn: A function is considered integrable on a set if it is almost everywhere strongly measurable on that set and has a finite integral of its pointwise norm.

MeasureTheory.LocallyIntegrableOn.integr.description: This theorem states that if a function is locally integrable over a certain interval and is asymptotically bounded by another function that is integrable over the same interval, then the first function is also integrable over that interval.

  {x : MeasurableSpace α} → Measure α → Set α → F →L[ℝ] F
MeasureTheory.weightedSMul.comment:
Given a set `s`, return the continuous linear map `fun x => (μ s).toReal • x`. The extension
of that set function through `setToL1` gives the Bochner integral of L1 functions.

explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.RingHom.id: This definition describes the identity ring homomorphism that maps each element of a semiring to itself.
explanatories.ENNReal.toReal: This definition describes a function that converts an extended nonnegative real number to a standard real number, returning the original number if it is finite and zero if it represents infinity.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.id: The identity map on a module over a semiring is defined as a continuous linear map that maps every element to itself.
explanatories.id: The identity function returns its input unchanged and can be used to explicitly assign a type to an expression for typeclass inference purposes.

MeasureTheory.weightedSMul.fullDefinition: def weightedSMul {_ : MeasurableSpace α} (μ : Measure α) (s : Set α) : F →L[ℝ] F :=   (μ s).toReal • ContinuousLinearMap.id ℝ F
MeasureTheory.weightedSMul.description: This definition describes a continuous linear map that returns a scaled version of a vector based on a measure assigned to a set, facilitating the computation of the Bochner integral for certain functions.

explanatories.Function.comp: Function composition combines two functions into a new function, where the output of the second function becomes the input of the first.

explanatories.Continuous.comp: The composition of two continuous functions in topological spaces is itself continuous.
explanatories.NNReal.coe_mk: This theorem states that the coercion of a nonnegative real number into a real number is equal to the original number itself.
explanatories.Iff.rfl: Any proposition is equivalent to itself.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto.comp: A theorem stating that the composition of two functions that tend to maps between respective filters also results in a function that tends to map from the original filter to the final one.
explanatories.Set.Subset.rfl: Every set is a subset of itself.
explanatories.Measurable.comp: This theorem establishes that if two functions are measurable, then their composition is also measurable.

  {E : Type u_7} [NormedAddCommGroup E] {f g : α → E} {p q : ℝ} (hpq : p.IsConjExponent q)
  (hf : Memℒp f (ENNReal.ofReal p) μ) (hg : Memℒp g (ENNReal.ofReal q) μ) :
  ∫ (a : α), ‖f a‖ * ‖g a‖ ∂μ ≤ (∫ (a : α), ‖f a‖ ^ p ∂μ) ^ (1 / p) * (∫ (a : α), ‖g a‖ ^ q ∂μ) ^ (1 / q)
MeasureTheory.integral_mul_norm_le_Lp_mu.comment:
Hölder's inequality for the integral of a product of norms. The integral of the product of two
norms of functions is bounded by the product of their `ℒp` and `ℒq` seminorms when `p` and `q` are
conjugate exponents.

explanatories.ENNReal.ofReal: This definition describes a function that converts a real number into the extended nonnegative real numbers, returning the number itself if it is nonnegative and zero if it is negative.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Memℒp: This definition characterizes a property of functions that indicates they are almost everywhere strongly measurable and integrates their norms to a finite value under a measure for finite exponents, or that their essential supremum is finite for the infinite exponent case.

MeasureTheory.integral_mul_norm_le_Lp_mu.description: This theorem establishes that the integral of the product of the norms of two functions is less than or equal to the product of their respective integrals raised to the powers determined by their conjugate exponents.

Filter.Tendsto.integral_sub_linear_isLit.comment:
Fundamental theorem of calculus for set integrals:
if `μ` is a measure that is finite at a filter `l` and
`f` is a measurable function that has a finite limit `b` at `l ⊓ ae μ`, then
`∫ x in s i, f x ∂μ = μ (s i) • b + o(μ (s i))` at a filter `li` provided that
`s i` tends to `l.smallSets` along `li`.
Since `μ (s i)` is an `ℝ≥0∞` number, we use `(μ (s i)).toReal` in the actual statement.

Often there is a good formula for `(μ (s i)).toReal`, so the formalization can take an optional
argument `m` with this formula and a proof of `(fun i => (μ (s i)).toReal) =ᶠ[li] m`. Without these
arguments, `m i = (μ (s i)).toReal` is used in the output.

explanatories.StronglyMeasurableAtFilter: This definition specifies the condition under which a function is considered strongly measurable at a given filter in relation to a certain measure, requiring it to be almost everywhere strongly measurable under restrictions defined by the filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.FiniteAtFilter: This definition states that a measure is considered finite at a filter if it is finite at some set contained in that filter or eventually finite at sets in the filter's collection of small sets.

Filter.Tendsto.integral_sub_linear_isLit.description: This theorem establishes that if a measurable function converges to a finite limit and a sequence of sets tends to small sets under a specified filter, then the integral of the function over those sets minus a linear term involving the measure converges to zero at that filter.

  {Y : Type u_2} {E : Type u_3} {F : Type u_4} {G : Type u_5} {𝕜 : Type u_6} [TopologicalSpace X] [TopologicalSpace Y]
  [MeasurableSpace Y] [OpensMeasurableSpace Y] {μ : Measure Y} [NontriviallyNormedField 𝕜] [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace ℝ E] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] [NormedAddCommGroup G] [NormedSpace 𝕜 G] [NormedSpace 𝕜 E]
  (L : F →L[𝕜] G →L[𝕜] E) {f : X → Y → G} {s : Set X} {k : Set Y} {g : Y → F} (hk : IsCompact k)

continuousOn_integral_bilinear_of_locall.comment:
Consider a parameterized integral `x ↦ ∫ y, L (g y) (f x y)` where `L` is bilinear,
`g` is locally integrable and `f` is continuous and uniformly compactly supported. Then the
integral depends continuously on `x`.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.IntegrableOn: A function is considered integrable on a set if it is almost everywhere strongly measurable on that set and has a finite integral of its pointwise norm.
explanatories.MeasurableSet.univ: This theorem confirms that the universal set is measurable in any measurable space.
explanatories.ContinuousOn: This defines a property indicating that a function between topological spaces is continuous at every point of a specified subset.
explanatories.IsCompact: This defines the property of a set within a topological space being compact, which requires that for any nontrivial filter containing the set, there is an element within the set such that every set in the filter intersects with every neighborhood of that element.

continuousOn_integral_bilinear_of_locall.description: This theorem states that the integral of a bilinear function, parameterized by a continuous function supported on a compact set, varies continuously with respect to its parameter when the integrand and its supporting measure are locally integrable.

explanatories.EReal: This definition introduces a type that represents the extended real numbers, which include negative infinity and positive infinity.

MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc.exists_le_lowerSemicontinuous_lintegral_ge.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [TopologicalSpace α]
  [MeasurableSpace α] [BorelSpace α] (μ : Measure α) [μ.WeaklyRegular] (f : α →ₛ ℝ≥0) {ε : ℝ≥0∞} (ε0 : ε ≠ 0) :
  ∃ g, (∀ (x : α), ↑f x ≤ g x) ∧ LowerSemicontinuous g ∧ ∫⁻ (x : α), ↑(g x) ∂μ ≤ ∫⁻ (x : α), ↑(↑f x) ∂μ + ε
MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc.exists_le_lower.comment:
Given a simple function `f` with values in `ℝ≥0`, there exists a lower semicontinuous
function `g ≥ f` with integral arbitrarily close to that of `f`. Formulation in terms of
`lintegral`.
Auxiliary lemma for Vitali-Carathéodory theorem `exists_lt_lower_semicontinuous_integral_lt`.

explanatories.LowerSemicontinuous: A function is lower semicontinuous if, in the vicinity of any point, its values do not drop below the value at that point minus any small positive amount.

MeasureTheory.SimpleFunc.exists_le_lower.description: For any non-negative simple function, there exists a lower semicontinuous function that bounds it from above and has an integral that can be made arbitrarily close to the integral of the original function.

A function `f` is called *interval integrable* with respect to a measure `μ` on an unordered
interval `a..b` if it is integrable on both intervals `(a, b]` and `(b, a]`. One of these
intervals is always empty, so this property is equivalent to `f` being integrable on
`(min a b, max a b]`.

Filter.Tendsto.eventually_intervalIntegr.code:
Filter.Tendsto.eventually_intervalIntegrable_ae.{u_1, u_3} {ι : Type u_1} {E : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  {f : ℝ → E} {μ : Measure ℝ} {l l' : Filter ℝ} (hfm : StronglyMeasurableAtFilter f l' μ) [TendstoIxxClass Ioc l l']
  [l'.IsMeasurablyGenerated] (hμ : μ.FiniteAtFilter l') {c : E} (hf : Tendsto f (l' ⊓ ae μ) (𝓝 c)) {u v : ι → ℝ}
  {lt : Filter ι} (hu : Tendsto u lt l) (hv : Tendsto v lt l) : ∀ᶠ (t : ι) in lt, IntervalIntegrable f μ (u t) (v t)
Filter.Tendsto.eventually_intervalIntegr.comment:
Let `l'` be a measurably generated filter; let `l` be a of filter such that each `s ∈ l'`
eventually includes `Ioc u v` as both `u` and `v` tend to `l`. Let `μ` be a measure finite at `l'`.

Suppose that `f : ℝ → E` has a finite limit at `l' ⊓ ae μ`. Then `f` is interval integrable on
`u..v` provided that both `u` and `v` tend to `l`.

Typeclass instances allow Lean to find `l'` based on `l` but not vice versa, so
`apply Tendsto.eventually_intervalIntegrable_ae` will generate goals `Filter ℝ` and
`TendstoIxxClass Ioc ?m_1 l'`.

explanatories.Set.Ioc: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-open and right-closed interval.
explanatories.IntervalIntegrable: A function is deemed interval integrable with respect to a measure on an unordered interval if it is integrable over both possible oriented intervals defined by the endpoints.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.ae: The "almost everywhere" filter represents the collection of sets that differ from a given set by at most a collection of co-null sets.
explanatories.StronglyMeasurableAtFilter: This definition specifies the condition under which a function is considered strongly measurable at a given filter in relation to a certain measure, requiring it to be almost everywhere strongly measurable under restrictions defined by the filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.FiniteAtFilter: This definition states that a measure is considered finite at a filter if it is finite at some set contained in that filter or eventually finite at sets in the filter's collection of small sets.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto.Ioc: A theorem stating that if two functions converge to a specified filter along a certain filter, then the image generated by their open interval function also converges to the small sets of another filter.

Filter.Tendsto.eventually_intervalIntegr.description: If a function is strongly measurable with respect to a measure and has a finite limit at a certain filter near a specific set of intervals, then it is interval integrable over those intervals as the endpoints of the intervals approach certain limits.

as `∫ x in Ioc a b, f x ∂μ - ∫ x in Ioc b a, f x ∂μ`. If `a ≤ b`, then it equals
`∫ x in Ioc a b, f x ∂μ`, otherwise it equals `-∫ x in Ioc b a, f x ∂μ`.

explanatories.Set.Ioc: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-open and right-closed interval.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto.Ioc: A theorem stating that if two functions converge to a specified filter along a certain filter, then the image generated by their open interval function also converges to the small sets of another filter.

intervalIntegral.fullDefinition: def intervalIntegral (f : ℝ → E) (a b : ℝ) (μ : Measure ℝ) : E :=   (∫ x in Ioc a b, f x ∂μ) - ∫ x in Ioc b a, f x ∂μ
intervalIntegral.description: The interval integral of a function over a specified range is defined as the difference between two integrals taken over intervals depending on the order of the bounds, with the integral being negated if the upper limit is less than the lower limit.

  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [CompleteSpace E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {a b : ℝ} {μ : Measure ℝ} {f : ℝ → E} [RCLike 𝕜]
  [NormedSpace 𝕜 E] [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] [CompleteSpace F] (L : E →L[𝕜] F)
  (hf : IntervalIntegrable f μ a b) : ∫ (x : ℝ) in a..b, L (f x) ∂μ = L (∫ (x : ℝ) in a..b, f x ∂μ)

explanatories.IntervalIntegrable: A function is deemed interval integrable with respect to a measure on an unordered interval if it is integrable over both possible oriented intervals defined by the endpoints.

continuous_linear_map.interval_integral_.description: The integral of a continuous linear map applied to a function over a specified interval is equal to the continuous linear map applied to the integral of the function over that same interval, provided the function is interval integrable.

intervalIntegral.integral_comp_mul_right.description: The integral of a function evaluated over a scaled interval is equal to the product of the scaling factor's inverse and the integral of the function over the original interval.

MeasureTheory.laverage.code: MeasureTheory.laverage.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {m0 : MeasurableSpace α} (μ : Measure α) (f : α → ℝ≥0∞) : ℝ≥0∞
MeasureTheory.laverage.comment:
Average value of an `ℝ≥0∞`-valued function `f` w.r.t. a measure `μ`, denoted `⨍⁻ x, f x ∂μ`.

It is equal to `(μ univ)⁻¹ * ∫⁻ x, f x ∂μ`, so it takes value zero if `μ` is an infinite measure. If
`μ` is a probability measure, then the average of any function is equal to its integral.

For the average on a set, use `⨍⁻ x in s, f x ∂μ`, defined as `⨍⁻ x, f x ∂(μ.restrict s)`. For the
average w.r.t. the volume, one can omit `∂volume`.

MeasureTheory.laverage.fullDefinition: noncomputable def laverage (f : α → ℝ≥0∞) := ∫⁻ x, f x ∂(μ univ)⁻¹ • μ

measure_theory.laverage.comment:
Average value of an `ℝ≥0∞`-valued function `f` w.r.t. a measure `μ`, denoted `⨍⁻ x, f x ∂μ`.

It is equal to `(μ univ)⁻¹ * ∫⁻ x, f x ∂μ`, so it takes value zero if `μ` is an infinite measure. If
`μ` is a probability measure, then the average of any function is equal to its integral.

For the average on a set, use `⨍⁻ x in s, f x ∂μ`, defined as `⨍⁻ x, f x ∂(μ.restrict s)`. For the
average w.r.t. the volume, one can omit `∂volume`.

MeasureTheory.average.code:
MeasureTheory.average.{u_1, u_2} {α : Type u_1} {E : Type u_2} {m0 : MeasurableSpace α} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace ℝ E] (μ : Measure α) (f : α → E) : E
MeasureTheory.average.comment:
Average value of a function `f` w.r.t. a measure `μ`, denoted `⨍ x, f x ∂μ`.

It is equal to `(μ univ).toReal⁻¹ • ∫ x, f x ∂μ`, so it takes value zero if `f` is not integrable or
if `μ` is an infinite measure. If `μ` is a probability measure, then the average of any function is
equal to its integral.

For the average on a set, use `⨍ x in s, f x ∂μ`, defined as `⨍ x, f x ∂(μ.restrict s)`. For the
average w.r.t. the volume, one can omit `∂volume`.

explanatories.MeasurableSet.univ: This theorem confirms that the universal set is measurable in any measurable space.

MeasureTheory.average.fullDefinition: noncomputable def average (f : α → E) :=   ∫ x, f x ∂(μ univ)⁻¹ • μ
MeasureTheory.average.description: This definition establishes the concept of the average value of a function with respect to a measure, stating that it corresponds to the integral of the function scaled by the reciprocal of the measure of the entire space, with specific behaviors in cases of non-integrability or infinite measure.

MeasureTheory.lintegral_comp_eq_lintegra.code:
MeasureTheory.lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_le_mul.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [MeasurableSpace α] {f : α → ℝ} {g : ℝ → ℝ}
  (μ : Measure α) (f_nn : 0 ≤ᶠ[ae μ] f) (f_mble : AEMeasurable f μ)
  (g_intble : ∀ t > 0, IntervalIntegrable g volume 0 t) (g_nn : ∀ᵐ (t : ℝ) ∂volume.restrict (Ioi 0), 0 ≤ g t) :
  ∫⁻ (ω : α), ENNReal.ofReal (∫ (t : ℝ) in 0 ..f ω, g t) ∂μ =
    ∫⁻ (t : ℝ) in Ioi 0, μ {a | t ≤ f a} * ENNReal.ofReal (g t)
MeasureTheory.lintegral_comp_eq_lintegra.comment:
The layer cake formula / **Cavalieri's principle** / tail probability formula:

Let `f` be a non-negative measurable function on a measure space. Let `G` be an
increasing absolutely continuous function on the positive real line, vanishing at the origin,
with derivative `G' = g`. Then the integral of the composition `G ∘ f` can be written as
the integral over the positive real line of the "tail measures" `μ {ω | f(ω) ≥ t}` of `f`
weighted by `g`.

Roughly speaking, the statement is: `∫⁻ (G ∘ f) ∂μ = ∫⁻ t in 0..∞, g(t) * μ {ω | f(ω) ≥ t}`.

See `MeasureTheory.lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_lt_mul` for a version with sets of the form
`{ω | f(ω) > t}` instead.

explanatories.ENNReal.ofReal: This definition describes a function that converts a real number into the extended nonnegative real numbers, returning the number itself if it is nonnegative and zero if it is negative.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict: This definition describes a method for limiting a measure to a specific subset, allowing for the analysis of the measure's properties exclusively within that subset.
explanatories.Set.Ioi: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than a specified element in a preorder structure, resulting in a left-open and right-infinite interval.
explanatories.AEMeasurable: This definition characterizes a function as almost everywhere measurable if it agrees with some measurable function on all but a negligible subset of its domain.

the integral over the positive real line of the "tail measures" `μ {ω | f(ω) > t}` of `f`

instead.

MeasureTheory.tendsto_integral_of_dominated_convergence.{u_1, u_3} {α : Type u_1} {G : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup G]
  [NormedSpace ℝ G] {m : MeasurableSpace α} {μ : Measure α} {F : ℕ → α → G} {f : α → G} (bound : α → ℝ)
  (F_measurable : ∀ (n : ℕ), AEStronglyMeasurable (F n) μ) (bound_integrable : Integrable bound μ)
  (h_bound : ∀ (n : ℕ), ∀ᵐ (a : α) ∂μ, ‖F n a‖ ≤ bound a)
  (h_lim : ∀ᵐ (a : α) ∂μ, Tendsto (fun n => F n a) atTop (𝓝 (f a))) :
  Tendsto (fun n => ∫ (a : α), F n a ∂μ) atTop (𝓝 (∫ (a : α), f a ∂μ))
MeasureTheory.tendsto_integral_of_domina.comment:
**Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem** provides sufficient conditions under which almost
everywhere convergence of a sequence of functions implies the convergence of their integrals.
We could weaken the condition `bound_integrable` to require `HasFiniteIntegral bound μ` instead
(i.e. not requiring that `bound` is measurable), but in all applications proving integrability
is easier.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable: A function is considered almost everywhere strongly measurable with respect to a measure if it is equal to the limit of a sequence of simple functions except on a set of measure zero.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Integrable: The definition describes a property indicating that a function is measurable and has a finite integral with respect to a specified measure.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.
explanatories.Filter.atTop: This definition introduces a filter that captures the behavior of elements approaching infinity in an ordered set, generated by all sets containing elements greater than or equal to any given element.

MeasureTheory.tendsto_integral_of_domina.description: Under certain conditions involving almost everywhere strong measurability and a bound that is integrable, almost everywhere convergence of a sequence of functions implies convergence of their integrals.

intervalIntegral.continuousWithinAt_of_d.comment:
Continuity of interval integral with respect to a parameter, at a point within a set.
Given `F : X → ℝ → E`, assume `F x` is ae-measurable on `[a, b]` for `x` in a
neighborhood of `x₀` within `s` and at `x₀`, and assume it is bounded by a function integrable
on `[a, b]` independent of `x` in a neighborhood of `x₀` within `s`. If `(fun x ↦ F x t)`
is continuous at `x₀` within `s` for almost every `t` in `[a, b]`
then the same holds for `(fun x ↦ ∫ t in a..b, F x t ∂μ) s x₀`.

interval_integral.continuous_of_dominate.comment:
Continuity of interval integral with respect to a parameter.
Given `F : X → ℝ → E`, assume each `F x` is ae-measurable on `[a, b]`,
and assume it is bounded by a function integrable on `[a, b]` independent of `x`.
If `(fun x ↦ F x t)` is continuous for almost every `t` in `[a, b]`
then the same holds for `(fun x ↦ ∫ t in a..b, F x t ∂μ) s x₀`.

intervalIntegral.measure_integral_sub_li.comment:
**Fundamental theorem of calculus-1**, local version for any measure.
Let filters `l` and `l'` be related by `TendstoIxxClass Ioc`.
If `f` has a finite limit `c` at `l' ⊓ ae μ`, where `μ` is a measure
finite at `l'`, then `∫ x in u..v, f x ∂μ = ∫ x in u..v, c ∂μ + o(∫ x in u..v, 1 ∂μ)` as both
`u` and `v` tend to `l`.

See also `measure_integral_sub_linear_isLittleO_of_tendsto_ae` for a version assuming
`[intervalIntegral.FTCFilter a l l']` and `[MeasureTheory.IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ]`. If `l` is one
of `𝓝[≥] a`, `𝓝[≤] a`, `𝓝 a`, then it's easier to apply the non-primed version.  The primed version
also works, e.g., for `l = l' = atTop`.

We use integrals of constants instead of measures because this way it is easier to formulate
a statement that works in both cases `u ≤ v` and `v ≤ u`.

explanatories.Set.Ioc: This definition denotes the set of elements that are strictly greater than one given element and less than or equal to another in a preorder structure, forming a left-open and right-closed interval.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.FiniteAtFilter: This definition states that a measure is considered finite at a filter if it is finite at some set contained in that filter or eventually finite at sets in the filter's collection of small sets.
explanatories.StronglyMeasurableAtFilter: This definition specifies the condition under which a function is considered strongly measurable at a given filter in relation to a certain measure, requiring it to be almost everywhere strongly measurable under restrictions defined by the filter.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.ae: The "almost everywhere" filter represents the collection of sets that differ from a given set by at most a collection of co-null sets.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto.Ioc: A theorem stating that if two functions converge to a specified filter along a certain filter, then the image generated by their open interval function also converges to the small sets of another filter.

intervalIntegral.measure_integral_sub_li.description: This theorem demonstrates that under certain conditions, the difference between the integral of a function and the integral of a constant over a variable interval tends to zero relative to the integral of the measure of that interval as the interval bounds approach a limit.

intervalIntegral.measure_integral_sub_li.comment:
**Fundamental theorem of calculus-1**, local version for any measure.

Let filters `l` and `l'` be related by `[intervalIntegral.FTCFilter a l l']`; let `μ` be a locally
finite measure.  If `f` has a finite limit `c` at `l' ⊓ ae μ`, then
`∫ x in u..v, f x ∂μ = ∫ x in u..v, c ∂μ + o(∫ x in u..v, 1 ∂μ)` as both `u` and `v` tend to `l`.

See also `measure_integral_sub_linear_isLittleO_of_tendsto_ae'` for a version that also works, e.g.,
for `l = l' = Filter.atTop`.

We use integrals of constants instead of measures because this way it is easier to formulate
a statement that works in both cases `u ≤ v` and `v ≤ u`.

explanatories.StronglyMeasurableAtFilter: This definition specifies the condition under which a function is considered strongly measurable at a given filter in relation to a certain measure, requiring it to be almost everywhere strongly measurable under restrictions defined by the filter.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.ae: The "almost everywhere" filter represents the collection of sets that differ from a given set by at most a collection of co-null sets.

intervalIntegral.measure_integral_sub_li.description: This theorem establishes that the difference between the integral of a function over an interval and the integral of a constant over the same interval behaves like a small perturbation relative to the integral of the length of that interval as the endpoints converge to a specified limit.

intervalIntegral.measure_integral_sub_integral_sub_linear_isLittleO_of_tendsto_ae.{u_1, u_3} {ι : Type u_1}
  {E : Type u_3} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] {f : ℝ → E} {a b : ℝ} {ca cb : E} {la la' lb lb' : Filter ℝ}
  {lt : Filter ι} {μ : Measure ℝ} {ua va ub vb : ι → ℝ} [FTCFilter a la la'] [FTCFilter b lb lb']
  [IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ] (hab : IntervalIntegrable f μ a b) (hmeas_a : StronglyMeasurableAtFilter f la' μ)
  (hmeas_b : StronglyMeasurableAtFilter f lb' μ) (ha_lim : Tendsto f (la' ⊓ ae μ) (𝓝 ca))
  (hb_lim : Tendsto f (lb' ⊓ ae μ) (𝓝 cb)) (hua : Tendsto ua lt la) (hva : Tendsto va lt la) (hub : Tendsto ub lt lb)
  (hvb : Tendsto vb lt lb) :
  (fun t =>
      ∫ (x : ℝ) in va t..vb t, f x ∂μ - ∫ (x : ℝ) in ua t..ub t, f x ∂μ -
        (∫ (x : ℝ) in ub t..vb t, cb ∂μ - ∫ (x : ℝ) in ua t..va t, ca ∂μ)) =o[lt]
    fun t => ‖∫ (x : ℝ) in ua t..va t, 1 ∂μ‖ + ‖∫ (x : ℝ) in ub t..vb t, 1 ∂μ‖
intervalIntegral.measure_integral_sub_in.comment:
**Fundamental theorem of calculus-1**, strict derivative in both limits for a locally finite
measure.

Let `f` be a measurable function integrable on `a..b`. Let `(la, la')` be a pair of
`intervalIntegral.FTCFilter`s around `a`; let `(lb, lb')` be a pair of `intervalIntegral.FTCFilter`s
around `b`. Suppose that `f` has finite limits `ca` and `cb` at `la' ⊓ ae μ` and `lb' ⊓ ae μ`,
respectively.
Then `∫ x in va..vb, f x ∂μ - ∫ x in ua..ub, f x ∂μ =
  ∫ x in ub..vb, cb ∂μ - ∫ x in ua..va, ca ∂μ +
    o(‖∫ x in ua..va, (1:ℝ) ∂μ‖ + ‖∫ x in ub..vb, (1:ℝ) ∂μ‖)`
as `ua` and `va` tend to `la` while `ub` and `vb` tend to `lb`.

| ------- | ----     | ---     | ----     |
| `Iic a` | `𝓝[≤] a` | `Iic b` | `𝓝[≤] b` |
| `Ici a` | `𝓝[>] a` | `Ici b` | `𝓝[>] b` |

  [CompleteSpace E] {f : ℝ → E} {ca cb : E} {la lb : Filter ℝ} {a b : ℝ} (hf : IntervalIntegrable f volume a b)
  {s t : Set ℝ} [FTCFilter a (𝓝[s] a) la] [FTCFilter b (𝓝[t] b) lb] (hmeas_a : StronglyMeasurableAtFilter f la volume)
  (hmeas_b : StronglyMeasurableAtFilter f lb volume) (ha : Tendsto f (la ⊓ ae volume) (𝓝 ca))
  (hb : Tendsto f (lb ⊓ ae volume) (𝓝 cb)) :
  HasFDerivWithinAt (fun p => ∫ (x : ℝ) in p.1 ..p.2, f x) ((snd ℝ ℝ ℝ).smulRight cb - (fst ℝ ℝ ℝ).smulRight ca)
    (s ×ˢ t) (a, b)
interval_integral.integral_has_fderiv_wi.comment:
Let `f` be a measurable function integrable on `a..b`. The function `(u, v) ↦ ∫ x in u..v, f x`
has derivative `(u, v) ↦ v • cb - u • ca` within `s × t` at `(a, b)`, where
`s ∈ {Iic a, {a}, Ici a, univ}` and `t ∈ {Iic b, {b}, Ici b, univ}` provided that `f` tends to `ca`
and `cb` almost surely at the filters `la` and `lb` from the following table.

| `s`     | `la`     | `t`     | `lb`     |
| ------- | ----     | ---     | ----     |
| `Iic a` | `𝓝[≤] a` | `Iic b` | `𝓝[≤] b` |
| `Ici a` | `𝓝[>] a` | `Ici b` | `𝓝[>] b` |
| `{a}`   | `⊥`      | `{b}`   | `⊥`      |
| `univ`  | `𝓝 a`    | `univ`  | `𝓝 b`    |

explanatories.StronglyMeasurableAtFilter: This definition specifies the condition under which a function is considered strongly measurable at a given filter in relation to a certain measure, requiring it to be almost everywhere strongly measurable under restrictions defined by the filter.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto: A definition stating that a function converges from one filter to another if the preimage of every neighborhood in the second filter is a neighborhood in the first filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.ae: The "almost everywhere" filter represents the collection of sets that differ from a given set by at most a collection of co-null sets.
explanatories.IntervalIntegrable: A function is deemed interval integrable with respect to a measure on an unordered interval if it is integrable over both possible oriented intervals defined by the endpoints.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.MeasureSpace.volume: This definition introduces a specific measure associated with a measure space, referred to as volume.
explanatories.ContinuousLinearMap.smulRight: The construction defines a continuous linear map that takes a scalar-valued linear map and an element from a module, producing a new linear map by scaling the output by the given element.
explanatories.Continuous.fst: This theorem establishes that the first component of a continuous mapping from one topological space to a product space remains continuous when the mapping is restricted to that component.
explanatories.Continuous.snd: This theorem states that if a function from one topological space to a product of two other topological spaces is continuous, then the projection onto the second component of that product is also continuous.
explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.HasFDerivWithinAt: A function has a specified continuous linear derivative at a point within a set if its behavior around that point can be approximated by the linear map in the limit as the input approaches the point from within the set.

interval_integral.integral_has_fderiv_wi.description: This theorem states that if a measurable function is integrable on a specified interval and tends to specific limits almost surely at designated filters, then the derivative of the integral function at a point within a certain set equals the difference of the function values at the endpoints, each scaled by unit vectors.

intervalIntegral.integral_hasDerivWithin.comment:
Fundamental theorem of calculus: if `f : ℝ → E` is integrable on `a..b` and `f x` has a finite
limit `c` almost surely as `x` tends to `b` from the right or from the left,
then `u ↦ ∫ x in a..u, f x` has right (resp., left) derivative `c` at `b`.

MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_of_has.code:
MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_of_hasFDerivWithinAt_off_countable.{u} {E : Type u} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E] {n : ℕ} (a b : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) (hle : a ≤ b)
  (f : (Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) → Fin (n + 1) → E) (f' : (Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) → (Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) →L[ℝ] Fin (n + 1) → E)
  (s : Set (Fin (n + 1) → ℝ)) (hs : s.Countable) (Hc : ContinuousOn f (Set.Icc a b))
  (Hd : ∀ x ∈ (Set.univ.pi fun i => Set.Ioo (a i) (b i)) \ s, HasFDerivAt f (f' x) x)
  (Hi : IntegrableOn (fun x => ∑ i : Fin (n + 1), (f' x) (e i) i) (Set.Icc a b) volume) :
  ∫ (x : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ) in Set.Icc a b, ∑ i : Fin (n + 1), (f' x) (e i) i =
    ∑ i : Fin (n + 1),
      ((∫ (x : Fin n → ℝ) in Set.Icc (a ∘ i.succAbove) (b ∘ i.succAbove), f (i.insertNth (b i) x) i) -
        ∫ (x : Fin n → ℝ) in Set.Icc (a ∘ i.succAbove) (b ∘ i.succAbove), f (i.insertNth (a i) x) i)
MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_of_has.comment:
**Divergence theorem** for Bochner integral. If `f : ℝⁿ⁺¹ → Eⁿ⁺¹` is continuous on a rectangular
box `[a, b] : Set ℝⁿ⁺¹`, `a ≤ b`, is differentiable on its interior with derivative
`f' : ℝⁿ⁺¹ → ℝⁿ⁺¹ →L[ℝ] Eⁿ⁺¹` and the divergence `fun x ↦ ∑ i, f' x eᵢ i` is integrable on `[a, b]`,
where `eᵢ = Pi.single i 1` is the `i`-th basis vector, then its integral is equal to the sum of
integrals of `f` over the faces of `[a, b]`, taken with appropriate signs.

Moreover, the same is true if the function is not differentiable at countably many
points of the interior of `[a, b]`.

We represent both faces `x i = a i` and `x i = b i` as the box
`face i = [a ∘ Fin.succAbove i, b ∘ Fin.succAbove i]` in `ℝⁿ`, where
`Fin.succAbove : Fin n ↪o Fin (n + 1)` is the order embedding with range `{i}ᶜ`. The restrictions
of `f : ℝⁿ⁺¹ → Eⁿ⁺¹` to these faces are given by `f ∘ backFace i` and `f ∘ frontFace i`, where
`backFace i = Fin.insertNth i (a i)` and `frontFace i = Fin.insertNth i (b i)` are embeddings
`ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ⁺¹` that take `y : ℝⁿ` and insert `a i` (resp., `b i`) as `i`-th coordinate.

We represent both faces `x i = a i` and `x i = b i` as the box
`face i = [a ∘ Fin.succAbove i, b ∘ Fin.succAbove i]` in `ℝⁿ`, where
`Fin.succAbove : Fin n ↪o Fin (n + 1)` is the order embedding with range `{i}ᶜ`. The restrictions
of `f : ℝⁿ⁺¹ → Eⁿ⁺¹` to these faces are given by `f ∘ backFace i` and `f ∘ frontFace i`, where
`backFace i = Fin.insertNth i (a i)` and `frontFace i = Fin.insertNth i (b i)` are embeddings
`ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ⁺¹` that take `y : ℝⁿ` and insert `a i` (resp., `b i`) as `i`-th coordinate.

MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_prod_Icc_of_hasFDerivWithinAt_off_countable_of_le.{u} {E : Type u}
  [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E] (f g : ℝ × ℝ → E) (f' g' : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ × ℝ →L[ℝ] E)

  (Hdg : ∀ x ∈ Set.Ioo a.1 b.1 ×ˢ Set.Ioo a.2 b.2 \ s, HasFDerivAt g (g' x) x)
  (Hi : IntegrableOn (fun x => (f' x) (1, 0) + (g' x) (0, 1)) (Set.Icc a b) volume) :

    (((∫ (x : ℝ) in a.1 ..b.1, g (x, b.2)) - ∫ (x : ℝ) in a.1 ..b.1, g (x, a.2)) + ∫ (y : ℝ) in a.2 ..b.2, f (b.1, y)) -

MeasureTheory.integral_divergence_prod_I.comment:
**Divergence theorem** for functions on the plane along rectangles. It is formulated in terms of
two functions `f g : ℝ × ℝ → E` and an integral over `Icc a b = [a.1, b.1] × [a.2, b.2]`, where
`a b : ℝ × ℝ`, `a ≤ b`. When thinking of `f` and `g` as the two coordinates of a single function
`F : ℝ × ℝ → E × E` and when `E = ℝ`, this is the usual statement that the integral of the
divergence of `F` inside the rectangle equals the integral of the normal derivative of `F` along the
boundary.

See also `MeasureTheory.integral2_divergence_prod_of_hasFDerivWithinAt_off_countable` for a
version that does not assume `a ≤ b` and uses iterated interval integral instead of the integral
over `Icc a b`.

MeasureTheory.integral2_divergence_prod_of_hasFDerivWithinAt_off_countable.{u} {E : Type u} [NormedAddCommGroup E]
  [NormedSpace ℝ E] [CompleteSpace E] (f g : ℝ × ℝ → E) (f' g' : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ × ℝ →L[ℝ] E) (a₁ a₂ b₁ b₂ : ℝ)
  (s : Set (ℝ × ℝ)) (hs : s.Countable) (Hcf : ContinuousOn f ([[a₁, b₁]] ×ˢ [[a₂, b₂]]))
  (Hcg : ContinuousOn g ([[a₁, b₁]] ×ˢ [[a₂, b₂]]))
  (Hdf : ∀ x ∈ Set.Ioo (min a₁ b₁) (max a₁ b₁) ×ˢ Set.Ioo (min a₂ b₂) (max a₂ b₂) \ s, HasFDerivAt f (f' x) x)
  (Hdg : ∀ x ∈ Set.Ioo (min a₁ b₁) (max a₁ b₁) ×ˢ Set.Ioo (min a₂ b₂) (max a₂ b₂) \ s, HasFDerivAt g (g' x) x)
  (Hi : IntegrableOn (fun x => (f' x) (1, 0) + (g' x) (0, 1)) ([[a₁, b₁]] ×ˢ [[a₂, b₂]]) volume) :
  ∫ (x : ℝ) in a₁..b₁, ∫ (y : ℝ) in a₂..b₂, (f' (x, y)) (1, 0) + (g' (x, y)) (0, 1) =
    (((∫ (x : ℝ) in a₁..b₁, g (x, b₂)) - ∫ (x : ℝ) in a₁..b₁, g (x, a₂)) + ∫ (y : ℝ) in a₂..b₂, f (b₁, y)) -

`f g : ℝ × ℝ → E` and iterated integral `∫ x in a₁..b₁, ∫ y in a₂..b₂, _`, where

`F : ℝ × ℝ → E × E` and when `E = ℝ`, this is the usual statement that the integral of the
divergence of `F` inside the rectangle with vertices `(aᵢ, bⱼ)`, `i, j =1,2`, equals the integral of
the normal derivative of `F` along the boundary.

CircleIntegrable.code: CircleIntegrable.{u_1} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] (f : ℂ → E) (c : ℂ) (R : ℝ) : Prop
CircleIntegrable.comment:
We say that a function `f : ℂ → E` is integrable on the circle with center `c` and radius `R` if
the function `f ∘ circleMap c R` is integrable on `[0, 2π]`.

Note that the actual function used in the definition of `circleIntegral` is
`(deriv (circleMap c R) θ) • f (circleMap c R θ)`. Integrability of this function is equivalent
to integrability of `f ∘ circleMap c R` whenever `R ≠ 0`.

explanatories.IntervalIntegrable: A function is deemed interval integrable with respect to a measure on an unordered interval if it is integrable over both possible oriented intervals defined by the endpoints.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.MeasureSpace.volume: This definition introduces a specific measure associated with a measure space, referred to as volume.

CircleIntegrable.fullDefinition: def CircleIntegrable (f : ℂ → E) (c : ℂ) (R : ℝ) : Prop :=   IntervalIntegrable (fun θ : ℝ => f (circleMap c R θ)) volume 0 (2 * π)
CircleIntegrable.description: A function is considered circle integrable if the composition of this function with a specific mapping from angles to points on a circle is integrable over the interval from zero to two pi.

The function `fun z ↦ (z - w) ^ n`, `n : ℤ`, is circle integrable on the circle with center `c`

cauchyPowerSeries.code:
cauchyPowerSeries.{u_1} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℂ E] (f : ℂ → E) (c : ℂ) (R : ℝ) :
  FormalMultilinearSeries ℂ ℂ E
cauchyPowerSeries.comment:
The power series that is equal to
$\frac{1}{2πi}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
  \oint_{|z-c|=R} \left(\frac{w-c}{z - c}\right)^n \frac{1}{z-c}f(z)\,dz$ at
`w - c`. The coefficients of this power series depend only on `f ∘ circleMap c R`, and the power
series converges to `f w` if `f` is differentiable on the closed ball `Metric.closedBall c R` and
`w` belongs to the corresponding open ball. For any circle integrable function `f`, this power
series converges to the Cauchy integral for `f`.

explanatories.Complex.I: This defines the imaginary unit as a complex number.
explanatories.FormalMultilinearSeries: A formal multilinear series is defined as a collection of multilinear maps that relate vectors from a source space to a target space over a specified ring.
explanatories.ContinuousMultilinearMap.mkPiRing: This definition describes a continuous multilinear map from a space of indexed scalars to a module that computes the product of its components, scaled by a fixed reference element.

cauchyPowerSeries.fullDefinition: def cauchyPowerSeries (f : ℂ → E) (c : ℂ) (R : ℝ) : FormalMultilinearSeries ℂ ℂ E := fun n =>   ContinuousMultilinearMap.mkPiRing ℂ _ <|     (2 * π * I : ℂ)⁻¹ • ∮ z in C(c, R), (z - c)⁻¹ ^ n • (z - c)⁻¹ • f z
cauchyPowerSeries.description: The cauchyPowerSeries definition describes a power series generated from a function evaluated along a circle in the complex plane, which converges to the function's value if the function is differentiable within a certain radius.

Complex.circleTransform.code:
Complex.circleTransform.{u_1} {E : Type u_1} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℂ E] (R : ℝ) (z w : ℂ) (f : ℂ → E)
  (θ : ℝ) : E
Complex.circleTransform.comment:
Given a function `f : ℂ → E`, `circleTransform R z w f` is the function mapping `θ` to
`(2 * ↑π * I)⁻¹ • deriv (circleMap z R) θ • ((circleMap z R θ) - w)⁻¹ • f (circleMap z R θ)`.

If `f` is differentiable and `w` is in the interior of the ball, then the integral from `0` to
`2 * π` of this gives the value `f(w)`.

explanatories.deriv: This definition provides the derivative of a function at a specific point, returning the derivative if it exists and zero otherwise.

Complex.circleTransform.fullDefinition: def circleTransform (f : ℂ → E) (θ : ℝ) : E :=   (2 * ↑π * I)⁻¹ • deriv (circleMap z R) θ • (circleMap z R θ - w)⁻¹ • f (circleMap z R θ)
Complex.circleTransform.description: This definition describes a transformation of a complex-valued function that maps an angle on a circle to a value in a normed space, and under certain conditions, integrates to yield the function's value at a specified point within the disk.

MeasureTheory.integral_Ioi_of_hasDerivAt.comment:
**Fundamental theorem of calculus-2**, on semi-infinite intervals `(a, +∞)`.
When a function has a limit at infinity `m`, and its derivative is integrable, then the
integral of the derivative on `(a, +∞)` is `m - f a`. Version assuming differentiability
on `(a, +∞)` and continuity at `a⁺`.

Note that such a function always has a limit at infinity,
see `tendsto_limUnder_of_hasDerivAt_of_integrableOn_Ioi`.

on `[a, +∞)`.

see `tendsto_limUnder_of_hasDerivAt_of_integrableOn_Ioi`.

  (hderiv : ∀ x ∈ Iio a, HasDerivAt f (f' x) x) (f'int : IntegrableOn f' (Iic a) volume) (hf : Tendsto f atBot (𝓝 m)) :
  ∫ (x : ℝ) in Iic a, f' x = f a - m
MeasureTheory.integral_Iic_of_hasDerivAt.comment:
**Fundamental theorem of calculus-2**, on semi-infinite intervals `(-∞, a)`.
When a function has a limit `m` at `-∞`, and its derivative is integrable, then the
integral of the derivative on `(-∞, a)` is `f a - m`. Version assuming differentiability
on `(-∞, a)` and continuity at `a⁻`.

see `tendsto_limUnder_of_hasDerivAt_of_integrableOn_Iic`.

If a continuous function `c` realizes its maximum at a unique point `x₀` in a compact set `s`,
then the sequence of functions `(c x) ^ n / ∫ (c x) ^ n` is a sequence of peak functions
concentrating around `x₀`. Therefore, `∫ (c x) ^ n * g / ∫ (c x) ^ n` converges to `g x₀` if `g` is

  {hm : MeasurableSpace α} {μ : Measure α} [TopologicalSpace α] [BorelSpace α] [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]
  {g : α → E} {x₀ : α} {s : Set α} [CompleteSpace E] [MetrizableSpace α] [IsLocallyFiniteMeasure μ] [μ.IsOpenPosMeasure]
  (hs : IsCompact s) {c : α → ℝ} (hc : ContinuousOn c s) (h'c : ∀ y ∈ s, y ≠ x₀ → c y < c x₀) (hnc : ∀ x ∈ s, 0 ≤ c x)

tendsto_set_integral_pow_smul_of_unique_.comment:
If a continuous function `c` realizes its maximum at a unique point `x₀` in a compact set `s`,
then the sequence of functions `(c x) ^ n / ∫ (c x) ^ n` is a sequence of peak functions
concentrating around `x₀`. Therefore, `∫ (c x) ^ n * g / ∫ (c x) ^ n` converges to `g x₀` if `g` is
continuous on `s`.

If a sequence of peak functions `φᵢ` converges uniformly to zero away from a point `x₀` and its
integral on some finite-measure neighborhood of `x₀` converges to `1`, and `g` is integrable and
has a limit `a` at `x₀`, then `∫ φᵢ • g` converges to `a`.

tendsto_integral_comp_smul_smul_of_integ.comment:
Consider a nonnegative function `φ` with integral one, decaying quickly enough at infinity.
Then suitable renormalizations of `φ` form a sequence of peak functions around the origin:
`∫ (c ^ d * φ (c • x)) • g x` converges to `g 0` as `c → ∞` if `g` is continuous at `0`
and integrable.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.AbsolutelyContinuo: This theorem states that a measure is absolutely continuous with respect to another measure if the measure of any measurable set that has zero measure under the second measure also has zero measure under the first measure.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.VectorMeasure.MutuallySing: Two vector measures are mutually singular if there exists a measurable set such that one measure is zero on all measurable subsets within it while the other measure is zero on all measurable subsets outside of it.

MeasureTheory.SignedMeasure.toJordanDeco.fullDefinition: def toJordanDecomposition (s : SignedMeasure α) : JordanDecomposition α :=   let i := s.exists_compl_positive_negative.choose   let hi := s.exists_compl_positive_negative.choose_spec   { posPart := s.toMeasureOfZeroLE i hi.1 hi.2.1     negPart := s.toMeasureOfLEZero iᶜ hi.1.compl hi.2.2     posPart_finite := inferInstance     negPart_finite := inferInstance     mutuallySingular := by       refine ⟨iᶜ, hi.1.compl, ?_, ?_⟩       -- Porting note: added `← NNReal.eq_iff`       · rw [toMeasureOfZeroLE_apply _ _ hi.1 hi.1.compl]; simp [← NNReal.eq_iff]       · rw [toMeasureOfLEZero_apply _ _ hi.1.compl hi.1.compl.compl]; simp [← NNReal.eq_iff] }

MeasureTheory.SignedMeasure.toSignedMeasure_toJordanDecomposition.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} [MeasurableSpace α]
  (s : SignedMeasure α) : s.toJordanDecomposition.toSignedMeasure = s
MeasureTheory.SignedMeasure.toSignedMeas.comment:
**The Jordan decomposition theorem**: Given a signed measure `s`, there exists a pair of
mutually singular measures `μ` and `ν` such that `s = μ - ν`. In this case, the measures `μ`
and `ν` are given by `s.toJordanDecomposition.posPart` and
`s.toJordanDecomposition.negPart` respectively.

Note that we use `MeasureTheory.JordanDecomposition.toSignedMeasure` to represent the
signed measure corresponding to
`s.toJordanDecomposition.posPart - s.toJordanDecomposition.negPart`.

MeasureTheory.SignedMeasure.toSignedMeas.description: This theorem demonstrates that converting a signed measure to its Jordan decomposition and then back to a signed measure yields the original signed measure itself.

measure_theory.measure.rn_deriv_lt_top.description: This theorem asserts that the Radon-Nikodym derivative of a sigma-finite measure with respect to another measure is finite almost everywhere with respect to that second measure.

MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_singularPart.code:

  (hf : Measurable f) (hs : s ⟂ₘ ν) (hadd : μ = s + ν.withDensity f) : s = μ.singularPart ν
MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_singularPart.comment:
Given measures `μ` and `ν`, if `s` is a measure mutually singular to `ν` and `f` is a
measurable function such that `μ = s + fν`, then `s = μ.singularPart μ`.

This theorem provides the uniqueness of the `singularPart` in the Lebesgue decomposition theorem,
while `MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_rnDeriv` provides the uniqueness of the
`rnDeriv`.

explanatories.Measurable: This definition describes a function between measurable spaces as measurable if it preserves the measurability of sets by ensuring that the preimage of any measurable set is also measurable.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.withDensity: This definition introduces a new measure constructed by weighting an existing measure with a non-negative, measurable function over a measurable set.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.singularPart: This definition characterizes a measure that represents the singular part of one measure with respect to another, returning either this singular measure or the zero measure if no decomposition exists.

MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_singularPart.description: This theorem establishes that if a measure is mutually singular to another and is expressed as the sum of that measure and a weighted version of the second measure, then it is equal to the singular part of the first measure with respect to the second measure.

MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_withDensity_rnD.comment:
Given measures `μ` and `ν`, if `s` is a measure mutually singular to `ν` and `f` is a
measurable function such that `μ = s + fν`, then `f = μ.rnDeriv ν`.

This theorem provides the uniqueness of the `rnDeriv` in the Lebesgue decomposition
theorem, while `MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_singularPart` provides the uniqueness of the

terms of the functions is given in `eq_rnDeriv`.

MeasureTheory.Measure.exists_positive_of.code:
MeasureTheory.Measure.exists_positive_of_not_mutuallySingular.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} {m : MeasurableSpace α}
  (μ ν : Measure α) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [IsFiniteMeasure ν] (h : ¬μ ⟂ₘ ν) :
  ∃ ε,
    0 < ε ∧
      ∃ E,
        MeasurableSet E ∧
          0 < ν E ∧ VectorMeasure.restrict 0 E ≤ VectorMeasure.restrict (μ.toSignedMeasure - (ε • ν).toSignedMeasure) E
MeasureTheory.Measure.exists_positive_of.comment:
If two finite measures `μ` and `ν` are not mutually singular, there exists some `ε > 0` and
a measurable set `E`, such that `ν(E) > 0` and `E` is positive with respect to `μ - εν`.

This lemma is useful for the Lebesgue decomposition theorem.

MeasureTheory.Measure.haveLebesgueDecomp.comment:
Any pair of finite measures `μ` and `ν`, `HaveLebesgueDecomposition`. That is to say,
there exist a measure `ξ` and a measurable function `f`, such that `ξ` is mutually singular
with respect to `ν` and `μ = ξ + ν.withDensity f`.

This is not an instance since this is also shown for the more general σ-finite measures with
`MeasureTheory.Measure.haveLebesgueDecomposition_of_sigmaFinite`.
MeasureTheory.Measure.haveLebesgueDecomp.description: This theorem asserts that any pair of finite measures possesses a Lebesgue decomposition, wherein one measure can be expressed as the sum of a mutually singular measure and a version of the other measure weighted by a measurable function.

explanatories.Measurable: This definition describes a function between measurable spaces as measurable if it preserves the measurability of sets by ensuring that the preimage of any measurable set is also measurable.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.withDensity: This definition introduces a new measure constructed by weighting an existing measure with a non-negative, measurable function over a measurable set.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.singularPart: This definition characterizes a measure that represents the singular part of one measure with respect to another, returning either this singular measure or the zero measure if no decomposition exists.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.rnDeriv: This definition describes a measurable function that represents the Radon-Nikodym derivative of one measure with respect to another, returning this derivative function or the zero function if no decomposition exists.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.mutuallySingular_s: This theorem asserts that the singular part of one measure with respect to another is orthogonal to the second measure, indicating mutual singularity.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.singularPart_add_r: This theorem states that when one measure has a Lebesgue decomposition with respect to another, it can be expressed as the sum of its singular part and a component weighted by the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the first measure with respect to the second.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.sum: This definition describes the sum operation for an indexed family of measures in a measurable space, resulting in a new measure.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.withDensity_tsum: This theorem demonstrates that the measure weighted by the sum of a countable collection of non-negative measurable functions is equal to the sum of the measures weighted by each function individually.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.sum_add_sum: This theorem demonstrates that the sum of measures over a collection is equal to the measure of the sum of corresponding elements, establishing a distributive property for measures across addition.
explanatories.HasCompl.compl: A function that returns the complement of an element in a set or lattice structure.
explanatories.Set: This defines a set as a collection of elements belonging to a specific type.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict: This definition describes a method for limiting a measure to a specific subset, allowing for the analysis of the measure's properties exclusively within that subset.
explanatories.lt_of_le_of_lt: This theorem asserts that in a preorder, if one element is less than or equal to a second element and the second element is strictly less than a third, then the first element is also strictly less than the third.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.measurable_spanningSets: This theorem establishes that the set of spanning sets associated with a sigma-finite measure is itself measurable.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.measure_spanningSets_lt_to: This theorem asserts that in a sigma-finite measure space, the measure of a specified set derived from the spanning sets is always finite.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.measure_mono: If one set is a subset of another, then the measure of the first set is less than or equal to the measure of the second set for any measure that adheres to the properties of an outer measure class.
explanatories.MeasurableSet: This definition specifies a condition for a set to be considered measurable within a given measurable space.
explanatories.Set.indicator: The definition describes a function that outputs a specified value for an element if it is in a given set, and returns zero otherwise.
explanatories.Measurable.indicator: The indicator function of a measurable set, based on a measurable function, is also measurable.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.withDensity_indicator: This theorem establishes that the measure obtained by weighting with the indicator function on a measurable set is equal to the measure restricted to that set and then weighted by the original function.
explanatories.Filter.EventuallyEq.symm: A theorem asserting that if two functions are equal almost everywhere with respect to a filter, then they are also equal almost everywhere in the reverse order with respect to that filter.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.VectorMeasure.restrict: This definition describes a method for restricting a vector measure to a specific subset of a measurable space.
explanatories.MeasurableSet.compl: This theorem asserts that if a set is measurable within a given measurable space, then its complement is also measurable in the same space.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.HaveLebesgueDecomp: This theorem states that if every finite measure has a Lebesgue decomposition with respect to another measure, then any s-finite measure also has a Lebesgue decomposition with respect to that measure.
explanatories.disjointed: This definition describes a sequence that is formed by subtracting each element from the next in an original sequence, resulting in a unique disjoint sequence that retains the same partial suprema as the original.
explanatories.MeasurableSet.disjointed: This theorem states that if a collection of measurable sets is disjoint and each set in the collection is measurable, then their union is also measurable.
explanatories.disjointed_le: This theorem asserts that the disjoint sequence formed from an original sequence is always less than or equal to the original sequence.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.MutuallySingular.s: The sum of a collection of measures is mutually singular with respect to another measure if and only if each individual measure in the collection is mutually singular with respect to that measure.

explanatories.MeasureTheory.Measure.MutuallySingular.s: This theorem asserts that if two measures are mutually singular, then the singular part of one measure with respect to another is also mutually singular to the second measure.
explanatories.MeasureTheory.sum_restrict_disjointed_sp: This theorem states that the sum of measures restricted to a collection of disjoint sets from a spanning family equals the original measure when the measure used for spanning is sigma-finite.

MeasureTheory.Measure.haveLebesgueDecomp.fullDefinition: nonrec instance (priority := 100) haveLebesgueDecomposition_of_sigmaFinite     [SFinite μ] [SigmaFinite ν] : HaveLebesgueDecomposition μ ν := by   wlog hμ : IsFiniteMeasure μ generalizing μ   · exact .sfinite_of_isFiniteMeasure fun μ _ ↦ this μ ‹_›   -- Take a disjoint cover that consists of sets of finite measure `ν`.   set s : ℕ → Set α := disjointed (spanningSets ν)   have hsm : ∀ n, MeasurableSet (s n) := .disjointed <| measurable_spanningSets _   have hs : ∀ n, Fact (ν (s n) < ⊤) := fun n ↦     ⟨lt_of_le_of_lt (measure_mono <| disjointed_le ..) (measure_spanningSets_lt_top ν n)⟩   -- Note that the restrictions of `μ` and `ν` to `s n` are finite measures.   -- Therefore, as we proved above, these restrictions have a Lebesgue decomposition.   -- Let `ξ n` and `f n` be the singular part and the Radon-Nikodym derivative   -- of these restrictions.   set ξ : ℕ → Measure α := fun n : ℕ ↦ singularPart (.restrict μ (s n)) (.restrict ν (s n))   set f : ℕ → α → ℝ≥0∞ := fun n ↦ (s n).indicator (rnDeriv (.restrict μ (s n)) (.restrict ν (s n)))   have hfm (n : ℕ) : Measurable (f n) := by measurability   -- Each `ξ n` is supported on `s n` and is mutually singular with the restriction of `ν` to `s n`.   -- Therefore, `ξ n` is mutually singular with `ν`, hence their sum is mutually singular with `ν`.   have hξ : .sum ξ ⟂ₘ ν := by     refine MutuallySingular.sum_left.2 fun n ↦ ?_     rw [← ν.restrict_add_restrict_compl (hsm n)]     refine (mutuallySingular_singularPart ..).add_right (.singularPart ?_ _)     refine ⟨(s n)ᶜ, (hsm n).compl, ?_⟩     simp [hsm]   -- Finally, the sum of all `ξ n` and measure `ν` with the density `∑' n, f n`   -- is equal to `μ`, thus `(Measure.sum ξ, ∑' n, f n)` is a Lebesgue decomposition for `μ` and `ν`.   have hadd : .sum ξ + ν.withDensity (∑' n, f n) = μ := calc     .sum ξ + ν.withDensity (∑' n, f n) = .sum fun n ↦ ξ n + ν.withDensity (f n) := by       rw [withDensity_tsum hfm, Measure.sum_add_sum]     _ = .sum fun n ↦ .restrict μ (s n) := by       simp_rw [ξ, f, withDensity_indicator (hsm _), singularPart_add_rnDeriv]     _ = μ := sum_restrict_disjointed_spanningSets ..   exact ⟨⟨(.sum ξ, ∑' n, f n), by measurability, hξ, hadd.symm⟩⟩
